rationale: The speaker experiences the rod of divine fury; the psalm likewise petitions the Lord not to discipline him in anger.
source_text: I am the man who sees poverty under the rod of His fury against me.

target_units.text: Lord, do not rebuke me in Thy fury, nor discipline me in Thine anger.

rationale: Being led into darkness rather than light parallels Job's account of God placing darkness before his face amid confinement.
source_text: He took me and led me away into darkness, not light.

target_units.text: I have been walled in all around and cannot pass through; He placed darkness before my face.

rationale: The divine hand repeatedly turns against the speaker; the psalm similarly describes God's hand pressing upon the sufferer.
source_text: Indeed, against me He turned His hand all day.

target_units.text: For Thine arrows became lodged in me, and Thou didst press Thy hand upon me.

rationale: The source joins damaged flesh, skin and bones; Job likewise depicts flesh decaying within skin and bones in a disordered bodily image.
source_text: He made my flesh and my skin old; He shattered my bones.

target_units.text: My flesh decayed within my skin, and my bones are held in my teeth.

rationale: The source describes God building against and surrounding the speaker; Job likewise describes trials and ambushers surrounding him on his roads.
source_text: He built against me, surrounded my head and toiled.

target_units.text: His trials came together against me on my roads; men lying in wait encircled me.

rationale: Both describe being made to dwell in dark places like people long dead, presenting present affliction through the imagery of death.
source_text: He made me dwell in dark places like the dead of ages.

target_units.text: For the enemy pursued my soul, brought my life low to the ground, made me sit in dark places like those long dead.

rationale: The source cannot go out from the enclosure built against him; the psalm likewise says the sufferer was handed over and did not go out.
source_text: He built against me, and I will not go out; He made my bronze heavy.

target_units.text: Thou didst remove my acquaintances far from me; they made me an abomination to themselves. I was handed over and did not go out.

rationale: The source cries while God blocks prayer; the psalm similarly describes crying by day without being heard.
source_text: Indeed, I will cry and call out; He blocked my prayer.

target_units.text: My God, I will cry by day, and Thou wilt not hear, and by night, and not to folly for me.

rationale: Built-up roads and blocked paths prevent movement in the source; Job likewise says he is walled in and cannot pass through.
source_text: He built up my roads, blocked my paths and troubled them.

target_units.text: I have been walled in all around and cannot pass through; He placed darkness before my face.

rationale: God is pictured as a waiting bear and hidden lion in the source; Hosea likewise describes divine confrontation through predatory cats and a distressed bear.
source_text: He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hidden places.

target_units.text: I will be like a panther to them and like a leopard along the Assyrians’ road.
I will meet them like a bear in distress and tear open their heart’s enclosure. There forest lion cubs will devour them; field beasts will tear them apart.

rationale: Both describe the speaker as made desolate by divine action; the earlier lament also describes being turned backward amid entrapment.
source_text: He pursued me when I turned away and brought me to a stop; He made me desolate.

target_units.text: From His height He sent fire; He brought it down into my bones. He spread a net for my feet; He turned me backward. He made me desolate, suffering pain all day long.

rationale: The source is fixed as the target of a drawn bow; Job likewise says God set him up like a target after tearing him apart.
source_text: He drew His bow and fixed me as a target for a missile.

target_units.text: While I was at peace, He scattered me; He took me by the hair and tore me apart, and set me up like a target.

rationale: Arrows enter the kidneys in the source; Job depicts attackers surrounding him with spears and striking his kidneys without sparing.
source_text: He drove the arrows of His quiver into my kidneys.

target_units.text: They surrounded me with spears, striking my kidneys without sparing; they poured my gall onto the earth.

rationale: The speaker becomes his people's laughingstock and daily psalm; the psalmist likewise becomes a proverb and the subject of wine-drinkers' songs.
source_text: I became a laughingstock to all my people, their psalm all day.

target_units.text: I made sackcloth my garment, and became a proverb to them.
Those sitting in the gate talked against me, and wine-drinkers sang about me.

rationale: God fills the speaker with bitterness and gall; Jeremiah similarly announces God feeding the people distresses and giving them gall-water to drink.
source_text: He filled me with bitterness and made me drunk with gall.

target_units.text: therefore thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Behold, I will feed them distresses and make them drink gall-water,

rationale: The source is fed ashes amid bodily humiliation; the psalm likewise depicts eating ashes like bread as an expression of affliction.
source_text: He knocked out my teeth with a pebble and fed me ashes.

target_units.text: For I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping,

rationale: The source's soul is driven from peace; the psalm likewise says there is no peace for the sufferer's bones under divine anger.
source_text: He drove my soul away from peace; I forgot good things.

target_units.text: There is no healing in my flesh because of Thine anger; there is no peace for my bones because of my sins.

rationale: The speaker declares his hope from the Lord perished; Job similarly describes God cutting off his hope like a tree.
source_text: I said, “My victory has perished, and my hope from the Lord.”

target_units.text: He tore me apart all around, and I was gone; He cut off my hope like a tree.

rationale: The remembered bitterness and gall explicitly return to the bitter nourishment described earlier in the chapter.
source_text: I remembered, from my poverty and my persecution, my bitterness and gall.

target_units.text: He filled me with bitterness and made me drunk with gall.

rationale: The soul remembers and broods in the source; the psalm joins a troubled heart and despondent spirit to remembering earlier days and meditating on God's works.
source_text: My soul will remember and brood over me.

target_units.text: My spirit grew despondent within me; within me my heart was troubled.
I remembered ancient days and meditated on all Thy works; I was pondering the works of Thy hands.

rationale: The speaker deliberately sets a matter in his heart and resolves to endure; the psalm similarly addresses the grieving soul with an instruction to hope in God.
source_text: I will set this in my heart; therefore I will endure.

target_units.text: Why are you deeply grieved, soul, and why do you disturb me? Hope in God, for I will thank Him: my God is the salvation of my face.

rationale: The source calls the Lord good to those who wait and seek; the psalm joins confidence in seeing His good things with repeated instruction to wait for Him.
source_text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul that will seek Him as good

target_units.text: I believe that I will see the Lord’s good things in the land of the living.
Wait for the Lord; act courageously, and let your heart be strong, and wait for the Lord.

rationale: Quiet endurance for the Lord's salvation corresponds to the psalm's submitting soul that locates its salvation and support in God.
source_text: and will endure and be quiet for the Lord’s salvation.

target_units.text: Will my soul not submit to God? For from Him is my salvation.
For He is my God and my Savior, my supporter; I shall certainly not be shaken any further.

rationale: Taking a yoke in youth is called good; Sirach likewise urges youthful instruction and portrays accepting wisdom through fetters, a neck collar and a carried burden.
source_text: It is good for a man when he takes up a yoke in his youth.

target_units.text: Child, choose instruction from your youth, and until your hair is gray you will find wisdom.
Approach her like one who plows and sows, and wait for her good fruits. For you will labor a little in her cultivation and soon eat from her produce.
How very harsh she is to the uninstructed! The fainthearted will not remain with her.
She will be upon him like a heavy testing stone, and he will not delay throwing her away.
For wisdom is according to her name, and she is not manifest to many.
Listen, child, and receive my judgment; do not reject my counsel.
Put your feet into her fetters and your neck into her collar.
Place your shoulder beneath her and carry her, and do not resent her bonds.

rationale: The source sits alone and silent under his burden; Jeremiah likewise sits alone before God's hand because he is filled with bitterness.
source_text: He will sit alone and be silent, because he has taken it upon himself.

target_units.text: I did not sit in their gathering as they played, but I was reverent before Thy hand. I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness.

rationale: The source gives his cheek to the striker and receives reproach; Isaiah's speaker likewise gives his cheeks to slaps and refuses to turn from shame.
source_text: He will give his cheek to the one striking him; he will be filled with reproaches.

target_units.text: I have given my back to scourges and my cheeks to slaps. I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.

relationship: answer to a parallel lament question
rationale: The source denies that the Lord rejects forever; the psalm asks whether rejection and the withholding of mercy can last forever.
source_text: For the Lord will not reject for ever.

target_units.text: “Will the Lord reject for the ages, and not again take pleasure?
Or will He cut off His mercy to the end, from generation to generation?
Or will God forget to show pity, or hold His compassions shut in His wrath?” Diapsalma.

rationale: The One who humbled will show abundant mercy in the source; the psalm likewise combines abundant mercy with the assurance that God's anger does not persist forever.
source_text: For the One who humbled will have compassion according to His abundant mercy.

target_units.text: The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy.
He will not be angry to the end, nor maintain wrath for ever.
He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our lawless deeds,
for according to heaven’s height above the earth, the Lord strengthened His mercy toward those who fear Him.
As far as the east is distant from the west, He removed our lawless deeds from us.
As a father has compassion on children, the Lord had compassion on those who fear Him,

rationale: Humbling prisoners underfoot belongs to the actions disavowed in the source's following lines; the psalm instead presents the Lord as releasing people in fetters.
source_text: To humble under one’s feet all the prisoners of the earth,

target_units.text: who does justice for those wronged, who gives food to the hungry. The Lord releases those in fetters.

rationale: Turning aside a person's judgment before the Most High is condemned in this sequence; Exodus expressly forbids perverting the poor person's judgment.
source_text: to turn aside a man’s judgment before the face of the Most High,

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.

rationale: The source denies divine authorization for condemning a person in the described unjust judgment; Exodus forbids unrighteous charges and killing the innocent and righteous.
source_text: to condemn a person when he is judged—the Lord did not say to do this.

target_units.text: You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.

relationship: parallel reception of good and calamity
rationale: The source asks whether calamities and good come from the Most High; Job likewise asks whether recipients of God's good things should also bear bad things.
source_text: will not calamities and good come from the mouth of the Most High?

target_units.text: He looked at her and said, “You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we received good things from the Lord’s hand, shall we not bear the bad things?” In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin at all with his lips before God.

rationale: Examining the people's way leads to a call to return to the Lord; Joel likewise calls the people to turn to God with their whole hearts.
source_text: Our way was searched and examined; let us return to the Lord.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

rationale: The source raises hearts upon hands toward heaven; the earlier prayer likewise joins pouring out the heart before God with lifting hands to Him.
source_text: Let us lift our hearts upon our hands to the Exalted One in heaven.

target_units.text: Rise, exult in the night at the beginning of your watch! Pour out your heart like water before the Lord. Lift your hands to Him for the lives of your infants, who weaken with hunger at the head of every way out.

rationale: Both confess communal sin and godlessness in prayer; Daniel also locates the resulting shame among Judah, Jerusalem and their leaders.
source_text: We have sinned and acted godlessly, and Thou wast not propitiated.

target_units.text: we have sinned, done wrong, acted impiously, fallen away, and transgressed Thy commandments and judgments,
and have not listened to Thy servants the prophets, to what they spoke in Thy name to our kings, our rulers, our fathers, and every nation upon the earth.

Righteousness belongs to Thee, Lord, but shame of face to us as on this day—to the people of Judah, those dwelling in Jerusalem, and all the people Israel, near and far, in all the countries where Thou didst scatter them because of the trespass they committed before Thee.
Master, shame of face belongs to us, to our kings, rulers, and fathers, because we have sinned against Thee.

rationale: The source accuses God of killing without sparing in fury; the earlier lament likewise describes slaughter without sparing on the day of His anger.
source_text: Thou didst cover Thyself with fury and drive us away; Thou didst kill without sparing.

target_units.text: Child and elder lay at the way out. My virgins and my young men went into captivity. With sword and famine Thou didst kill; on the day of Thine anger Thou didst slaughter without sparing.

rationale: The source says God placed the people in rejection among other peoples; the psalm likewise describes God making His people a reproach and ridicule among nations.
source_text: to close my eyes; Thou didst place us to be rejected among the peoples.

target_units.text: Thou madest us a reproach to our neighbors, scorn and ridicule to those around us.
Thou madest us a parable among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.

rationale: Both describe all the enemies opening their mouths against the afflicted people; the earlier passage expands the image with hissing and hostile triumph.
source_text: All our enemies opened their mouths against us.

target_units.text: All your enemies opened their mouths against you. They hissed and gnashed their teeth; they said, “We have swallowed her! Indeed, this is the day we expected; we found it, we saw it!”

rationale: The eye pours water at the people's shattering; the Jeremiah passage likewise asks for eyes as a fountain of tears to mourn the wounded daughter of the people.
source_text: My eye will bring down outpourings of water at the shattering of the daughter of my people.

target_units.text: Who will give my head water and my eyes a fountain of tears, and I will weep day and night for this people of Mine, for the wounded of the daughter of My people?

rationale: The speaker's eye was swallowed up, yet he will not be silent because there is no recovery; Jeremiah similarly commands unceasing tears for the people's painful crushing.
source_text: My eye was swallowed up, and I will not be silent, for there is no recovery,

target_units.text: And you will say this word to them: Bring tears down upon your eyes day and night, and let them not cease, because the daughter of My people was utterly crushed, with a very painful wound.

relationship: parallel appeal for a heavenly gaze
rationale: The source waits until the Lord bends down and sees from heaven; Isaiah likewise calls on Him to turn from heaven and see the people's need.
source_text: until the Lord bends down and sees from heaven.

target_units.text: Turn from heaven and see from Thy holy and glorious house. Where are Thy zeal and strength? Where is the abundance of Thy mercy and compassion, since Thou hast held back from us?

relationship: shared hunted-bird imagery with contrasting outcome
rationale: The source's enemies hunt him like a sparrow; the psalm pictures communal rescue as a little bird escaping hunters' shattered trap.
source_text: My enemies hunted and hunted me like a sparrow without cause.

target_units.text: Our soul was rescued like a little bird from the trap of hunters; the trap was shattered, and we were rescued.

rationale: The source describes his life put to death in a pit with a stone laid upon him; the psalm similarly describes being placed in the lowest pit and death's shadow.
source_text: They put my life to death in a pit and laid a stone upon me.

target_units.text: They put me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in death’s shadow.

rationale: Water passes over the speaker's head as he declares rejection; Jonah likewise links engulfing waters with feeling thrust away from God's eyes.
source_text: Water overflowed my head; I said, “I have been rejected.”

target_units.text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.
I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’
Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.

rationale: Calling the Lord from the lowest pit corresponds to the psalm's cry from the depths and appeal that God hear the voice of petition.
source_text: I called upon Thy name, Lord, from the lowest pit.

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. From the depths I have cried unto Thee, Lord.
Lord, hear my voice; let Thine ears be attentive to the voice of my petition.

rationale: The source asks God not to hide His ears from supplication; the psalm likewise asks His ears to attend to the voice of petition.
source_text: Thou didst hear my voice: “Do not hide Thine ears from my supplication.”

target_units.text: Lord, hear my voice; let Thine ears be attentive to the voice of my petition.

rationale: The source remembers God drawing near to help when called; the psalm likewise recounts a poor person's cry heard by the Lord and followed by rescue.
source_text: Thou didst draw near to help me on the day I called Thee; Thou didst say to me, “Do not fear.”

target_units.text: This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him; from all his afflictions He saved him.

rationale: The Lord judges the cases of the speaker's soul and redeems his life; the psalm similarly asks Him to judge a case, redeem and give life.
source_text: Thou didst judge the cases of my soul, Lord; Thou didst redeem my life.

target_units.text: Judge my case and redeem me; give me life because of Thy word.

relationship: parallel seeing and judging the sufferer's case
rationale: The source joins God's seeing troubles to His judging the case; the psalm likewise appeals to the Lord who has seen to attend and judge righteously.
source_text: Thou didst see my troubles, Lord; Thou didst judge my case.

target_units.text: Thou hast seen, Lord; do not remain silent. Lord, do not depart from me.
Awake, Lord, and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my case.
Judge me according to Thy righteousness, Lord my God; let them not rejoice over me.

rationale: God's seeing the enemies' vengeance and reasonings is paired with His hearing their reproach and reasonings, presenting complementary appeals to divine awareness.
source_text: Thou didst see all their vengeance in all their reasonings against me.

target_units.text: Thou didst hear their reproach, all their reasonings against me,

rationale: The source invokes God's hearing of enemies' reproach; the psalm similarly asks the Lord to remember the reproach directed by enemies at His servants and anointed.
source_text: Thou didst hear their reproach, all their reasonings against me,

target_units.text: Remember, Lord, the reproach of Thy servants, which I bore in my bosom from many nations,
with which Thine enemies reproached, Lord, with which they reproached the exchange of Thine anointed.

rationale: Hostile lips and meditations operate all day in the source; the psalm likewise describes enemies speaking vain things and meditating on deceptions all day.
source_text: the lips of those rising against me and their meditations against me all day,

target_units.text: Those seeking my soul used violence; those seeking evils for me spoke vain things and meditated on deceptions all day long.

rationale: The source draws God's attention to enemies' sitting and rising; the psalm similarly describes God's knowledge of the speaker's sitting and rising. The source's eyes are not replaced with song imagery.
source_text: their sitting and their rising; look upon their eyes.

target_units.text: Thou knewest my sitting and my rising; Thou didst understand my reasonings from afar.

rationale: The source anticipates the Lord repaying a recompense according to the adversaries' works; the psalm petitions for the same repayment according to the works of their hands.
source_text: Thou wilt repay them a recompense, Lord, according to the works of their hands.

target_units.text: Give them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their practices; give them according to the works of their hands; repay their recompense to them.

rationale: The source anticipates divine pursuit and destruction in anger; the psalm likewise asks God to pursue enemies in a storm, trouble them in wrath and bring them to ruin.
source_text: Thou wilt pursue in anger and consume them from beneath heaven, Lord.

target_units.text: so Thou wilt pursue them with Thy storm and trouble them in Thy wrath.
Fill their faces with dishonor, and they will seek Thy name, Lord.
Let them be ashamed and troubled for an age of an age; let them be abashed and perish,

rationale: Dimmed precious metals and holy stones poured out at the head of every way out belong with the earlier rejection of altar and sanctuary and the shattering of the city's defenses.
source_text: How the gold will grow dim, how the good silver will change! Holy stones were poured out at the head of every way out.

target_units.text: The Lord rejected His altar and shook off His sanctuary. He shattered the wall of her citadels in the enemy’s hand. They raised a shout in the Lord’s house as on a festival day.

rationale: The opening change in gold and scattered holy stones extends to Zion's precious sons, formerly valued as gold but now regarded as earthen vessels.
source_text: Zion’s precious sons, exalted in gold— how they were regarded as earthen vessels, works of a potter’s hands!

target_units.text: How the gold will grow dim, how the good silver will change! Holy stones were poured out at the head of every way out.

rationale: The thirsty nursing child and infants without bread recall the earlier children failing in the squares and asking their mothers for grain and wine.
source_text: The nursing child’s tongue clung to its throat with thirst. Infants asked for bread; there is no one to break it for them.

target_units.text: My eyes failed with tears; my heart was troubled. My glory was poured onto the ground at the shattering of the daughter of my people, as infant and nursing child failed in the city’s squares.
They said to their mothers, “Where are grain and wine?” They weakened like the wounded in the city’s squares, and their lives poured out into their mothers’ bosoms.

rationale: Those raised in luxury now wrap themselves in dung heaps; Job's sitting on a dung heap supplies a related image of bodily humiliation, without equating the two narratives.
source_text: Those who ate luxuries were destroyed at the ways out; those nursed upon scarlet wrapped themselves in dung heaps.

target_units.text: He took a potsherd to scrape off the discharge, and sat on the dung heap outside the city.

rationale: The comparison with Sodom's quickly accomplished overthrow points to the Genesis account of the Lord overturning Sodom and its surrounding country.
source_text: The lawlessness of the daughter of my people became greater than Sodom’s lawlessness, which was overthrown as in haste, and they did not labor their hands upon it.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

rationale: Skin clings to bones in the source's unrecognizable sufferers; the psalm likewise describes bone clinging to flesh amid groaning.
source_text: Their appearance grew darker than soot; they were unrecognized at the ways out. Their skin clung to their bones; they dried up and became like wood.

target_units.text: From the sound of my groaning, my bone clung to my flesh.

rationale: The source compares the sword's victims with famine's victims; Jeremiah likewise juxtaposes sword-wounded people in the plain with famine within the city.
source_text: Those wounded by the sword were better off than those wounded by famine; they went away pierced through, deprived of the fields’ produce.

target_units.text: If I go out to the plain, behold, those wounded by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, the pain of famine! For priest and prophet went to a land they did not know.

rationale: Women boiling their children as food correspond to the warning that severe enemy distress can drive even a delicate mother to consume her children.
source_text: The hands of compassionate women boiled their children; they became food for them at the shattering of the daughter of my people.

target_units.text: And you shall eat the offspring of your womb, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters whom the Lord your God has given you, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemy shall afflict you.
The tender and most delicate man among you shall look grudgingly upon his brother, and the wife of his bosom, and the children who remain unto him,
begrudging any of them the flesh of his children which he eats, because nothing is left unto him, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemies shall afflict you in all your cities.

And the tender and most delicate woman among you, whose foot has never ventured to tread upon the earth because of her delicacy and tenderness, shall look grudgingly upon the husband of her bosom, and her son, and her daughter,

and upon her afterbirth which comes forth from between her thighs, and the child whom she bears; for she shall eat them secretly for want of all things, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemy shall afflict you in all your cities.

rationale: The Lord's fury kindles fire that consumes Zion's foundations; the earlier lament likewise depicts His furious anger as fire consuming Jacob's surroundings.
source_text: The Lord completed His fury and poured out His furious anger. He kindled a fire in Zion, and it consumed her foundations.

target_units.text: In His furious anger He broke every horn of Israel. He turned back His right hand before the enemy and kindled a flame in Jacob like fire, consuming everything around.

relationship: contrast with false confidence in security
rationale: The unexpected entry of enemies into Jerusalem challenges assumptions of inviolability; Jeremiah had likewise warned that confidence in the Lord's temple would not prevent its destruction.
source_text: The kings of the earth, all who dwell in the inhabited world, did not believe that enemy and oppressor would enter through Jerusalem’s gates.

target_units.text: Do not put your confidence in yourselves on false words, because they will not benefit you at all when they say, ‘The Lord’s temple, the Lord’s temple it is.’
For if you truly correct your ways and practices and truly execute judgment between a man and his neighbor,
and do not oppress a newcomer, orphan, or widow, and do not shed innocent blood in this place, and do not follow foreign gods to your own harm,
then I will settle you in this place, in the land I gave your fathers, from age to age.
But if you have trusted false words from which you will receive no benefit,
and murder and commit adultery and steal and swear unjustly, and you burned incense to Baal and followed foreign gods whom you do not know, to your own harm,
and you came and stood before Me in the house over which My name has been called and said, ‘We have kept away, so as not to do all these abominations,’
is My house, over which My name has been called there, a robbers’ cave before you? And behold, I have seen, says the Lord.
For go to My place in Shiloh, where I formerly made My name dwell, and see what I did to it because of the evil of My people Israel.
And now, because you did all these works, and I spoke to you and you did not hear Me, and I called you and you did not answer,
I will also do to this house over which My name has been called, in which you have trusted, and to the place I gave you and your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.

rationale: The source attributes the disaster to prophets' sins, priests' injustice and righteous bloodshed; Micah likewise connects Jerusalem's bloodshed and corrupt priests and prophets to Zion's destruction.
source_text: It was because of her prophets’ sins and her priests’ injustices, those who shed righteous blood in her midst.

target_units.text: Hear these things now, leaders of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house, who abhor justice and twist all straight things,
you who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices!

Her leaders judged with gifts, her priests answered for wages and her prophets divined for silver; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Calamities will certainly not come upon us.”
Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

rationale: The source calls for distance from unclean people and describes their loss of residence; Leviticus similarly joins an unclean designation with dwelling apart. This does not identify the source's people as lepers.
source_text: Keep away from unclean people—call them—keep away, keep away! Do not touch, for they were set aflame and shaken. Say among the nations, “They will sojourn no longer.”

target_units.text: And he that has leprosy, in whom the lesion is, shall have his garments loosened and his head uncovered, and shall put a covering about his mouth, and shall be called unclean;
all the days in which the lesion is upon him, being unclean, he shall be unclean; he shall dwell apart; his dwelling shall be outside the camp.

relationship: parallel denial of respect to elders
rationale: The source reports no mercy to elders; Deuteronomy's threatening nation likewise refuses regard for the aged. The comparison concerns this clause, not the source's difficult statement about God's face.
source_text: The Lord’s face is their portion; He will look upon them no longer. They showed no respect to priests and no mercy to elders.

target_units.text: a nation shameless of countenance, which shall not regard the face of the aged, nor have mercy upon the young.

rationale: The people's eyes fail while awaiting a nation unable to save; Isaiah likewise condemns dependence on Egyptian help that cannot survive the Lord's intervention.
source_text: While we still existed, our eyes failed, looking vainly for our help. Keeping watch, we watched for a nation that does not save.

target_units.text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!
He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,
an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

rationale: The pursuers are swifter than heavenly eagles; Jeremiah similarly depicts an approaching enemy with horses swifter than eagles.
source_text: Those pursuing us became swifter than the eagles of heaven. They were kindled upon the mountains and lay in wait for us in the wilderness.

target_units.text: Behold, he will come up like a cloud, and his chariots like a storm; his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, because we suffer misery!

relationship: contrast exposing the limits of rulers
rationale: The captured anointed ruler had been expected to provide protective shade; the psalm warns that rulers cannot provide salvation and are themselves mortal, exposing the limits of such confidence.
source_text: The spirit of our face, the Lord’s anointed, was seized in their destructions, of whom we said, “In his shadow we will live among the nations.”

target_units.text: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men who have no salvation.
His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.

rationale: The source tells Idumea that the Lord's cup will pass to her too and she will become drunk; Obadiah likewise announces recompense upon the addressed enemy and drinking judgment extending to the nations.
source_text: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Idumea, dwelling upon the land! To you too the Lord’s cup will pass; you will become drunk and pour it out.

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.
For just as you drank on My holy mountain, all the nations will drink wine; they will drink and go down, and they will be as though they did not exist.

rationale: The source announces the end of Zion's lawlessness and promises no further deportation; Isaiah likewise comforts Jerusalem because her humiliation is fulfilled and her sin loosed.
source_text: Your lawlessness has ended, Daughter Zion; He will deport you no longer. He has visited your acts of lawlessness, Daughter Edom; He has uncovered your acts of ungodliness.

target_units.text: You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

rationale: The source asks the Lord to remember and see the people's reproach; the psalm likewise petitions Him to remember His servants' reproach borne from nations.
source_text: Remember, Lord, what has happened to us; look and see our reproach.

target_units.text: Remember, Lord, the reproach of Thy servants, which I bore in my bosom from many nations,

rationale: The people's houses and inheritance pass to strangers; Jeremiah similarly announces houses being transferred to others alongside fields and households.
source_text: Our inheritance has passed to outsiders, our houses to strangers.

target_units.text: And their houses will be transferred to others, fields and their wives together, because I will stretch out My hand against those dwelling in this land, says the Lord.

relationship: contrast of abandonment with divine care
rationale: The community describes itself as fatherless and its mothers as widows; the psalm identifies God as the Father of orphans and judge of widows, answering the stated vulnerability.
source_text: We have become orphans; there is no father; our mothers are like widows.

target_units.text: the Father of orphans and judge of widows, God in His holy place.

rationale: Pursuit, exhaustion and lack of rest in the source repeat the earlier account of exiled Judea finding no rest and being overtaken by pursuers.
source_text: We were pursued at our neck; we toiled and did not rest.

target_units.text: Judea was deported because of her humiliation and her great slavery. She dwelt among the nations; she found no rest. All her pursuers overtook her among those who afflicted her.

rationale: The source connects the people's present burden with departed fathers' lawlessness; Daniel likewise connects Jerusalem's reproach with both present sins and the fathers' acts of ignorance.
source_text: Our fathers sinned and no longer exist; we bore their lawless acts.

target_units.text: Master, according to Thy righteousness, let Thy wrath and anger turn away from Thy city Jerusalem, Thy holy mountain. Because of our sins and our fathers’ acts of ignorance, Jerusalem and Thy people, Lord, are a reproach among all around us.

rationale: Slaves rule the afflicted people in the source; the psalm likewise describes being handed into nations' hands and subjected to hostile masters. The target does not identify those masters as slaves.
source_text: Slaves ruled over us; there is no one to redeem us from their hand.

target_units.text: He handed them over into nations’ hands, and those hating them became their masters.
Their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled beneath their hands.

relationship: related danger of sword and famine
rationale: Obtaining bread risks death from the wilderness sword; Jeremiah likewise places sword wounds outside the city beside famine inside, presenting related conditions of dangerous subsistence.
source_text: At the risk of our lives we will bring in our bread, because of the sword of the wilderness.

target_units.text: If I go out to the plain, behold, those wounded by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, the pain of famine! For priest and prophet went to a land they did not know.

rationale: Famine leaves skin livid like an oven in the source; Job likewise describes darkened skin and bones scorched by heat, a related image of bodily distress.
source_text: Our skin turned livid like an oven; they shriveled because of famine’s storms.

target_units.text: My skin has darkened greatly, and my bones are scorched from heat.

relationship: parallel humiliation of women in Jerusalem's fall
rationale: The source mourns women's humiliation in Zion and Judah; Zechariah's account of Jerusalem's capture explicitly includes violated women amid plunder and captivity.
source_text: They humiliated women in Zion, virgins in Judah’s cities.

target_units.text: I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for war. The city will be captured, the houses plundered and the women violated. Half the city will go into captivity, but the remnant of My people will certainly not be destroyed from the city.

rationale: The source's elders receive no glory; the preceding lament likewise reports that elders received no mercy, repeating the collapse of regard for them.
source_text: Rulers were hung by their hands; elders were not glorified.

target_units.text: The Lord’s face is their portion; He will look upon them no longer. They showed no respect to priests and no mercy to elders.

rationale: Chosen men's songs cease alongside the departure of elders from the gate; Jeremiah likewise announces the end of joyful voices in Jerusalem's thoroughfares and Judah's cities.
source_text: Elders ceased from the gate, chosen men ceased from their songs.

target_units.text: And I will stop the sound of those rejoicing and the sound of those glad, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, from Judah’s cities and Jerusalem’s thoroughfares, because the whole land will become a desolation.

relationship: close reversal of joy into mourning
rationale: The source's dancing becomes mourning and heart's joy ends; Amos similarly announces festivals turning into mourning and songs into lamentation.
source_text: The joy of our heart ended; our dancing turned to mourning.

target_units.text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

rationale: The community's crown falls from its head; Job likewise describes God removing his crown together with his glory, expressing lost dignity.
source_text: The crown fell from our head; woe indeed to us, for we sinned!

target_units.text: He stripped glory from me and took the crown from my head.

relationship: repeated sorrow of heart and eyes
rationale: The sorrowful heart and dim eyes repeat the earlier joining of failing eyes and a troubled heart at the people's destruction.
source_text: For this our heart became sorrowful; for this our eyes grew dim,

target_units.text: My eyes failed with tears; my heart was troubled. My glory was poured onto the ground at the shattering of the daughter of my people, as infant and nursing child failed in the city’s squares.

rationale: Destroyed Zion traversed by foxes corresponds to Micah's warning that Zion would be plowed and the temple mountain become a forest grove.
source_text: because Mount Zion was destroyed; foxes passed through her.

target_units.text: Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

rationale: Both address the Lord as enduring forever and connect His permanence with generation after generation amid surrounding human affliction.
source_text: But Thou, Lord, wilt dwell for ever; Thy throne endures from generation to generation.

target_units.text: But Thou, Lord, remainest for ever, and Thy memorial is from generation to generation.

rationale: The source asks why God forgets and forsakes for so long; the psalm similarly asks why He turns away and forgets the people's poverty and affliction.
source_text: Why wilt Thou forget us for ever and forsake us for so many days?

target_units.text: Awake! Why dost Thou sleep, Lord? Arise, and do not thrust us away completely.
Why dost Thou turn Thy face away and forget our poverty and affliction?

rationale: Both ask God to turn the people back, treating their restoration as dependent on His action.
source_text: Turn us back unto Thee, O Lord, and we shall be turned back; and renew our days as before.

target_units.text: God, turn us back; make Thy face shine, and we shall be saved.

rationale: The source ends by declaring divine rejection and great anger; the psalm petitions the Lord not to thrust His people away completely, voicing the corresponding appeal.
source_text: For Thou hast utterly rejected us and hast been exceedingly angry with us.

target_units.text: Awake! Why dost Thou sleep, Lord? Arise, and do not thrust us away completely.
